title: From Cell Chemistry to Combat Power: A Mission-Driven Review of Battery-Dependent and Electrically Powered Military Systems
content: Military capability increasingly depends on electrical energy for sensing, communications, computing, autonomy, mobility, protection, electronic warfare, and electrically enabled weapons. However, the value of a battery or energy-storage technology cannot be judged from chemistry or cell-level energy density alone. This review develops a mission-driven framework linking cell chemistry → module/pack → power electronics and thermal management → platform integration → mission effect → operational energy and contested logistics. It distinguishes energy from power and organizes military systems into four analytical battery roles: battery-integral, battery-dependent, battery-buffered, and battery-secondary. The framework is applied across soldier systems, smart munitions, unmanned systems, tactical vehicles, naval platforms, and high-power electrically enabled systems. The review finds that no universal “best military battery” exists; technology selection must reflect mission duty cycle, power demand, environmental exposure, survivability, recharge or resupply conditions, and system integration. Cell-level advantages can be reduced by pack overhead, protection, thermal management, power conversion, degradation, maintainability, and logistics. The review also proposes a cross-level evidence framework that distinguishes cell, pack, platform, modeled, demonstrated, operational, and fielded evidence. These findings support a mission-driven transition roadmap and strategic implications for force design, acquisition, research priorities, and operational-energy planning.
